lessons.title: Sampling and collecting data
lessons.summary: Choose the data to collect, use a suitable sample, and interpret an investigation.
lessons.objective: Choose the data to collect, use a suitable sample, and interpret an investigation.
lessons.before: Some data are labels. Other data are numbers from counts or measurements.
lessons.ideas:
Categorical data name groups. A discrete count takes separate allowed values. A continuous measurement can fall anywhere in an interval.

Larger samples can reduce sampling variation. Choice of participants also matters.

Organise results in a table or chart. Compare rates rather than raw counts if the group sizes differ.
lessons.method:
Name the data type and show how the answer will be recorded.

Name both the group you want to describe and the people you actually sampled.

Explain what the results suggest and what another sample could check.
mistakes: A house number is a label, even though it is written with digits.
Asking many people from the same narrow group can still give a biased sample.
An unexpected result may come from sampling variation or a real difference.

examples.title: Choosing a type of data
examples.question:
A teacher asks 15 pupils how they travelled to school: by bus, car, bike or on foot.

  1. Classify the data being collected.

    [1]

  2. Suggest one clear instruction for gathering these data in the same way from everyone.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The answer names a category.

Categorical data

(b) Agree the definition and collect information the same way from everyone.

Ask each pupil for their main way of travelling on the same day.

examples.title: Checking who was asked
examples.question:
Two groups ask about enjoying board games. One asks 18 classmates in one room. The other chooses 33 pupils at random from a full school list.

  1. Which sample is more useful for estimating the views of the entire school?

    [2]

  2. Explain why asking many pupils from just one room could still give a biased result.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) A full-school selection can include different groups of pupils.

The larger number also makes one unusual answer less influential.

The random sample across the school

(b) A larger sample only helps if its selection also suits the question.

The chosen room may have different pupils or interests from other rooms.

examples.title: Testing a prediction with data
examples.question:
A pupil predicts that group A succeeds more often on a puzzle than group B. Each trial records either success or no success.

GroupTrialsRecorded successes
Group A3331
Group B3634

  1. Which group has the higher proportion of successes?

    [2]

  2. Does the evidence support the prediction? Suggest one follow-up before drawing a firm conclusion.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Group A succeeds in \(\frac{31}{33}\) of trials.

Group B succeeds in \(\frac{17}{18}\).

Both have 2 unsuccessful trials. Group B has more trials, so the unsuccessful share is smaller.

Group B

(b) Start with a question and a prediction. Collect results, represent the counts, then interpret them.

An increase in sample size may reduce sampling variation.

The prediction is not supported by these results. Repeat the same puzzle with larger groups selected in the same way.

lessons.title: Venn diagrams, Carroll diagrams and tables
lessons.summary: Record counts with tallies, complete two-way totals and sort items by two features.
lessons.objective: Record counts with tallies, complete two-way totals and sort items by two features.
lessons.before: Add one mark each time an observation belongs to a category. Count the marks to write a frequency.
lessons.ideas:
A frequency tells how many observations fit a value or category. Add the separate counts to find the total.

Use a row total or column total to find a missing entry. Both sets of totals give the same overall count.

Count the overlap once. An item outside both circles has neither feature.
lessons.method:
Check the total against the number of items collected.

Put a finger on the row and the column to find the correct cell.

Label both features and check all four counts add up.
mistakes: Read a group of five tally marks as five, even when the fifth is drawn across the other four.
The overall total needs every observation once, rather than all the totals added together.
An outside region is still part of the whole data set.

examples.question:
A group sorts counters by picture.

PictureFrequency
Flower6
Leaf4
Seed5

  1. How many counters are sorted altogether?

    [2]

  2. How many counters do not show a flower?

    [2]

  3. Explain how tally marks could be used to record the original sort.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Add the frequencies 6, 4 and 5.

\(15\).

(b) Include the two other categories.

\(9\).

(c) Tally marks can be counted afterwards to fill the frequency column.

Make a row for each picture. Add one tally per counter, with groups of five where possible.

examples.question:

ClassPrinted bookAudio bookTotal

  1. Complete the missing number.

    [2]

  2. How many pupils choose a printed book altogether?

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Class N has 4 pupils in the table.

Subtract its 2 printed books.

\(2\).

(b) Add the printed-book counts from class M and class N.

\(21\).

examples.title: Sorting with two features
examples.question:
Among 83 shapes, 12 are blue, 5 are triangles and 3 are both blue and triangles.

  1. How many shapes are neither blue nor triangles?

    [2]

  2. Show the four counts in either a Venn diagram or a Carroll diagram. Explain how both represent the same groups.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Blue only is 12 minus 3, or 9.

Triangle only is 5 minus 3, or 2.

Subtract the counts 9, 2 and 3 from 83.

\(69\).

(b) Each shape belongs in exactly one region or cell.

Blue only 9, triangle only 2, both 3, neither 69. On a Venn diagram use the overlap for both. In a Carroll table the both count goes in the Blue and Triangle cell.

lessons.title: Bar charts, pie charts and waffle diagrams
lessons.summary: Compare and choose displays for category counts, shares and grouped measurements.
lessons.objective: Compare and choose displays for category counts, shares and grouped measurements.
lessons.before: For each category, put the two group bars side by side if you want to compare their individual counts.
lessons.ideas:
A dual bar chart compares parts across groups. A compound bar stacks parts, showing a group total as well as its pieces.

A pie-chart angle is the category's fraction of 360°. In a 100-square waffle, each square represents 1%.

Use a time exactly on a boundary in the group that includes that value.
lessons.method:
Use the same scale and a clear key for both sets of bars.

Check that all slices together make a full turn, or all waffle shares give 100%.

State the units on the horizontal axis and the frequency on the vertical axis.
mistakes: A stacked bar starts the upper piece at the top of the lower piece. Use the thickness of the upper piece for its count.
The number of items is not automatically the angle in degrees.
If a group ends before 20, an exact reading of 20 belongs in the next group.

examples.title: Comparing two groups on a bar chart
examples.question:
These are the values labelled on a dual bar chart at a club.

ActivityTuesdayFriday
Sketching65
Sewing32

  1. What is the total attendance for both activities on Friday?

    [2]

  2. Explain why a dual bar chart could make the activity counts easier to compare than one separate chart for each day.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The Friday bars show 5 and 2.

\(7\).

(b) A compound or stacked bar makes the combined total easy to see. A dual bar chart shows detailed counts directly beside one another.

It puts the values for the same activity side by side on the same scale.

examples.title: Representing part of a whole
examples.question:
Out of 85 visitors to a museum, 19 chose the model room and 2 chose the art room. Each picks one room.

  1. Find the angle for the model room on a pie chart.

    [2]

  2. Explain how a waffle diagram with 100 squares could represent the same share.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The share is \(\frac{19}{85}\).

Multiply this share by 360°.

\(\frac{1368}{17}\) degrees.

(b) Use the closest whole number of squares if the percentage is not a whole number.

Shade about 22 of the 100 squares. Each square represents 1% of the visitors.

examples.title: Grouping continuous times
examples.question:
A class groups the time for a short task into three equal-width groups. These would give touching bars on a frequency diagram.

Time t (seconds)Number of trials
\(0\leq t<20\)10
\(20\leq t<40\)5
\(40\leq t<60\)11

  1. How many trials took less than 40 seconds?

    [2]

  2. Where does a measured time of exactly 20 seconds go? Explain your choice.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The first two groups count 10 and 5 trials.

\(15\).

(b) Read the inequality on both sides of 20.

lessons.title: Line graphs, scatter graphs and infographics
lessons.summary: Describe change, compare paired measurements and read a graphic with a key.
lessons.objective: Describe change, compare paired measurements and read a graphic with a key.
lessons.before: Read the time and the value at each point. The order of times matters for a line graph.
lessons.ideas:
A rise shows an increase, a fall shows a decrease and a horizontal section shows no change.

An upward pattern means larger values of one variable tend to go with larger values of the other.

Multiply the number of full icons by the key value. A partial icon shows the same fraction of the key.
lessons.method:
Use two real readings from the graph to support a statement.

Look at the axis labels and note any point far from the general pattern.

Look for a clear scale, readable labels and a title that says what was counted.
mistakes: A higher line does not always rise if it was even higher a little earlier.
A pattern alone does not tell which measurement, if either, causes the other.
If the icons use different scales, counting them without reading the key gives a misleading comparison.

  2. Describe the change before and after 10:00.

    [2]

Subtract the 11:00 reading, 8 cm.

\(5\) cm.

(b) The directions of the line segments show rise or fall.

examples.title: Checking the key of an infographic
examples.question:
A display counts badges. Every full icon shown represents 2 badges. The display key is the same for all colours.

ColourNumber of complete icons
Gold15
Silver6

  1. How many gold badges are represented?

    [2]

  2. Explain one way to make the display fair when comparing gold and silver.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) There are 15 whole icons for gold.

Multiply by 2 badges per icon.

\(30\).

(b) Making an icon larger to show a larger count can exaggerate how different the groups are.

Use the same icon size and the same number represented by one icon for both colours.

lessons.title: Averages and the range
lessons.summary: Calculate the mean, median, mode and range, and choose a summary that fits the question.
lessons.objective: Calculate the mean, median, mode and range, and choose a summary that fits the question.
lessons.before: Add all observations and imagine redistributing the total equally among them.
lessons.ideas:
The mean is the sum divided by the number of observations. The result need not be one of the original values.

The median can be more useful than the mean if a very high or low value would pull the mean away from most of the data.

The range is largest minus smallest. A low range shows the whole set is contained within a small interval.

For each row, multiply value by frequency. Add these totals and divide by the sum of the frequencies.
lessons.method:
Check that the mean lies between the smallest and largest values.

Show the ordered list and identify the central position or positions.

Explain which feature your chosen summary tells the reader about.

Check that your mean fits between the lowest and highest data values.
mistakes: Divide by the number of values, not by the largest number in the list.
Middle means middle after sorting, rather than the middle of the unsorted list.
The range is the size of a gap, rather than writing down both endpoint values.
The number of rows is not the number of observations. Use the total frequency.

examples.title: Summarising five measurements
examples.question:
Five sensor readings are 22, 9, 7, 11, 9.

  1. Find the mean.

    [2]

  2. Explain how the mean would change if the largest value rose by 5.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Add all five values. The sum is 58.

Divide the sum by the count, 5.

\(\frac{58}{5}\).

(b) Think about which positions or counts each summary uses.

The sum goes up by 5 and there are still 5 values, so the mean goes up by 1.

examples.title: Summarising five measurements
examples.question:
Five sensor readings are 35, 22, 20, 24, 22.

  1. Find the median.

    [2]

  2. Would the median change if the largest value increased? Explain.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Put the readings in order: 20, 22, 22, 24, 35.

Read the third value out of five.

\(22\).

(b) Think about which positions or counts each summary uses.

No. The third value stays the same when only the largest value increases.

examples.title: Summarising five measurements
examples.question:
Five sensor readings are 48, 35, 33, 37, 35.

  1. Find the range.

    [2]

  2. Find the mode and explain how the mode and range describe different features of the data.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The greatest value is 48 and the smallest is 33.

Subtract 33 from 48.

\(15\).

(b) Think about which positions or counts each summary uses.

The mode is 35, the most frequent value. The range is 15, the gap from the smallest to the largest value.

examples.title: Finding an average from a larger set
examples.question:
A club records completed rounds for 55 players. Every player belongs in one table row.

Count per playerPlayers

  1. Find the mean number of completed rounds.

    [2]

  2. Identify the mode or modes. Explain when the mode is helpful.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) For each row multiply rounds per player by the number of players.

Add these results for 225 rounds in total. Divide by the 55 players.

\(\frac{45}{11}\).

(b) The highest frequency is 24.

The most common round count is 5. The mode helps when you want to name a usual count that actually occurred.
